caveat: READY_FOR_HUMAN_REVIEW means structurally safe to send to a reviewer. It is not material alignment, not human review, and not publishable.

reviewLedger.learningGoal: You will form the Cartesian product of two sets, count its elements, and see why the order of the two sets matters.
representationRequirements: ordered-pair notation, grid or arrow diagram

reviewLedger.learningGoal: You will define a relation as a subset of a Cartesian product, and separate its domain, its codomain and its range.
You will decide whether a relation is a function by testing one condition: every element of the domain has exactly one image.
You will recognise the standard real functions by rule, domain, range and graph, and see why some of their graphs must be drawn in pieces.
You will add, subtract, multiply and divide real functions, and work out the domain of the result rather than assuming it.
You will feed the output of one function into another, and see why the order and the domain both need care.
You will tell a strict inequality from a weak one and say what its solution set is.
You will solve a linear inequality in one variable and draw its solution on a number line.
representationRequirements: number line with open and closed endpoints

reviewLedger.learningGoal: You will name the three coordinate planes and the eight octants, and say where a region of space lies.
You will read and plot an ordered triple and state the sign pattern of its octant.
You will derive the distance formula in space and use it to test geometric claims.
You will find the point that divides a segment in space in a given ratio.
You will shade the half-plane satisfying a two-variable inequality and find the region satisfying a system.
representationRequirements: half-plane region on a coordinate plane

reviewLedger.learningGoal: You will describe an angle as a rotation, read its sign as a direction, and recognise that many different angles can share one terminal side.
representationRequirements: rotation diagram with initial and terminal sides

reviewLedger.learningGoal: You will measure an angle by the arc it cuts on a circle, and convert exactly between degrees and radians in both directions.
representationRequirements: rotation diagram with initial and terminal sides

reviewLedger.learningGoal: You will define the six trigonometric functions from a point on the unit circle, so that they accept any real argument rather than only an acute angle.
You will work out the sign of each trigonometric function in each quadrant from the signs of the coordinates, rather than recalling a mnemonic.
representationRequirements: quadrant sign table and unit circle

reviewLedger.learningGoal: You will state the domain, range and period of each trigonometric function and read its graph, including where the curve must break.
You will derive the sine and cosine of a sum and a difference of two angles, and use them to find values the standard angles alone could not give.
You will deduce the double- and triple-angle identities and the sum-to-product forms from the sum and difference identities, rather than collecting them as separate formulas.
You will write the complete solution of a simple trigonometric equation as an infinite family parameterised by an integer, rather than as a single value.
You will write a complex number as a + ib, name its real and imaginary parts, and see why the real number line alone could not supply a square root of minus one.
You will add, subtract and multiply complex numbers by working on their parts, and see where the minus sign in multiplication comes from.
You will reduce any integer power of i using a cycle of four, and divide one complex number by another using the conjugate.
You will compute the modulus of a complex number exactly and connect it to the conjugate through the identity z times its conjugate equals the modulus squared.
You will place a complex number as a point on the plane and read the modulus as its distance from the origin.
You will fix a complex number by its distance from the origin and its direction, and convert between that description and the usual one.
You will find the roots of a real-coefficient quadratic whose discriminant is negative, and see that they form a conjugate pair.
You will measure the steepness of a line as a ratio of two changes, and see why a vertical line has no slope at all.
You will decide when two lines are parallel or perpendicular, and find the angle between them when they are neither.
You will write the equation of a line parallel to an axis, and build the point-slope form from the definition of slope rather than from memory.
You will write a line in three further forms and recognise that different equations can describe the same line.
You will describe a line by the perpendicular from the origin, and see how every form of a line reduces to one general equation.
representationRequirements: coordinate graph with perpendicular from origin

reviewLedger.learningGoal: You will find the shortest distance from a point to a line, and see why that distance does not depend on how the equation was written.
You will count the outcomes of a choice made in stages, without listing them all.
You will write and use factorial notation for the products that counting keeps producing.
You will derive the formula for the number of ordered arrangements of r objects chosen from n.
You will count arrangements when some objects are identical, and when some positions are fixed.
You will count selections where order does not matter, and derive nCr from nPr.
You will state the binomial theorem for a positive integral index and follow its proof by induction.
You will read a sequence from its rule and name the term at any position.
You will write the sum of a sequence’s terms in sigma notation and expand it again.
You will find the arithmetic mean of two numbers and insert arithmetic means between them.
You will recognise a geometric progression and find its term at any position.
You will derive and use the sum of the first n terms of a geometric progression.
You will decide when an infinite geometric series has a sum, and find it from the partial sums.
representationRequirements: limit of a sum; G.M. notation

reviewLedger.learningGoal: You will show that the arithmetic mean of two positive numbers is never less than their geometric mean.
You will use the closed forms for the sums of the first n natural numbers, their squares and their cubes.
You will see how one double cone produces four different curves, according to how a plane cuts it.
You will see what the four conics collapse to when the cutting plane passes through the vertex of the cone.
You will derive the equation of a circle from its distance definition, and read a centre and radius back out of one.
representationRequirements: coordinate diagram with centre and radius

reviewLedger.learningGoal: You will derive the standard equation of a parabola from its focus and directrix, and identify its vertex, axis and latus rectum.
representationRequirements: parabola diagram with focus and directrix

reviewLedger.learningGoal: You will derive both standard equations of an ellipse and see that the two are different orientations rather than rival formulas.
You will compute the eccentricity and latus rectum of an ellipse from its own parameters, exactly.
You will derive the standard equation of a hyperbola from a difference of distances, and see why it has two separate branches.
You will compute the eccentricity and latus rectum of a hyperbola exactly, and see why its eccentricity exceeds 1.
You will see how the slope between two points on a curve becomes a rate of change, and what happens as those points close together.
You will say what it means for a function to approach a value near a point, and see that this is a different question from its value at the point.
You will compute limits of polynomials and rational functions, including the case where a factor cancels and the original function still has a hole.
You will use the standard limits for trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic functions, and see why radian measure is essential to them.
You will define the derivative as the limit of a difference quotient and derive it from first principles.
You will derive and use the rules for differentiating sums, differences, products and quotients.
representationRequirements: derivative notation as used in the source

reviewLedger.learningGoal: You will differentiate a composite function using the chain rule.
You will explain why a measure of centre alone does not describe data, and name the measures of spread.
You will compute the range of a data set and state its limitation.
You will compute the mean deviation about the mean for ungrouped and grouped data.
You will compute the mean deviation about the median for ungrouped and grouped data.
You will compute the variance and standard deviation of ungrouped data and explain why deviations are squared.
You will compute the variance and standard deviation of a frequency distribution.
You will use the step-deviation method and show it agrees with the direct method.
You will describe a random experiment by listing its outcomes as a sample space in set notation.
You will describe an event as a subset of the sample space and say when it occurs.
You will build new events from old ones using not, and, or.
You will decide whether a collection of events is exhaustive, mutually exclusive, both or neither.
You will say what makes an assignment of numbers to outcomes a probability.
You will derive the favourable-over-total rule as the equally likely case of the axioms.
You will find the probability of not, and, or events from the event sets.
You will prove a statement about every natural number by checking one case and showing each case carries the next.
You will write a collection in roster form and in set-builder form, and see that the two can describe the very same set.
You will recognise when a description has no elements at all, and see why ∅ and {∅} are different sets.
You will decide whether a set is finite or infinite from the rule that defines it, not from how its roster is written.
You will decide whether two sets are equal by comparing membership, and see why order and repetition do not change a set.
You will decide whether one set is contained in another, and separate a subset from a proper subset.
representationRequirements: interval notation and the real line

reviewLedger.learningGoal: You will read and write open, closed and half-open intervals as subsets of the real numbers, and say exactly which endpoints belong.
representationRequirements: interval notation and the real line

reviewLedger.learningGoal: You will fix a universal set for a discussion and see that the same set sits inside different valid universes.
You will read a Venn diagram as a statement about membership, and say what each region of it means.
You will build the union and the intersection of two sets from membership conditions, and see why the or in union includes both.
You will form A \u2212 B from membership conditions and see why reversing the order gives a different set.
You will form the complement of a set relative to a declared universe, and derive De Morgan\u2019s laws rather than memorise them.
You will count the members of two overlapping sets by accounting for each region once, and see why the overlap must be subtracted.
